newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's truth probe seeks amnesty extension.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's truth probe seeks amnesty extension.

text.p: South Africa's truth commission, entering a key phase of its search for apartheid's criminals, said on Friday it would seek to widen its powers of amnesty.

Bishop Desmond Tutu, chairman of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, told a news conference the body would ask parliament to extend by three months the period during which crimes can be classified as political.

Legislation creating the commission sets December 1993 as the cut-off date for political crimes but Tutu said this should be extended to May 10, 1994, the date of President Nelson Mandela's inauguration as the country's first democratic leader.
"The commission views the December 1993 cut-off date as one arbitrarily determined by the fact that the interim constitution was adopted at that time," Tutu said.
"The participation in the commission's work of two important constituencies, those of the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC) and the Freedom Front (FF), would be enhanced by such a decision," he added.

Black and white activists from the radical left and right conducted a spate of bombings and other attacks in the first months of 1994 in a last-ditch attempt to disrupt elections in late April of that year.
The commission, which began its work in April this year, has so far mainly heard from victims of human rights abuses or their relatives but is now beginning to grill perpetrators.
Five senior security branch officers from the apartheid era have volunteered to tell the commission about dozens of political killings in exchange for amnesty.
Two of them, Brigadier Jan Cronje and Captain Jacques Hechter, appeared in a Pretoria magistrate's court on Friday charged with 27 counts of murder and four counts of attempted murder.
They were granted bail and told to appear again in March, but the cases against them would be dropped if their amnesty application to the truth commission succeeds.

They are being investigated by a Pretoria-based attorney general who is conducting a separate probe into human rights abuses by police and military intelligence. State prosecutors have complained that the commission's amnesty process is hampering their work.
The commission has issued subpoenas to four senior police chiefs from the apartheid years to force them to appear before its investigators.

It was set up by Mandela last year to draw as complete a picture as possible of human rights abuses by all sides in the 33-year armed struggle against white minority governments, in the hope that this would aid reconciliation.

Tutu has said the failed prosecution of former defence minister Magnus Malan, acquitted last week of being behind a 1987 massacre of 13 blacks, showed that a "Nuremberg Trials" approach would not work in South Africa. He said his commission, which emphasises voluntary confession, had a better chance of getting to the truth.
